clinicalPearls: A Gram-negative bacillus inhabiting soil and stagnant water in tropical and subtropical regions, often producing a violet pigment (violacein) on culture
Infection typically follows exposure of broken skin to contaminated soil or water, sometimes after minor trauma
Presentation ranges from localised skin pustules or abscesses to fulminant necrotising sepsis with multiple visceral abscesses, especially in the liver and lungs
Recurrent or severe disease should prompt evaluation for chronic granulomatous disease and other defects of neutrophil oxidative killing
The organism is frequently resistant to many beta-lactams, so agents such as fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, aminoglycosides or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are usually preferred
Prolonged combination therapy with drainage of abscesses is often required to prevent relapse
Untreated or late-recognised systemic infection has a high fatality rate
reference.pathophysiology: Chromobacterium violaceum is an environmental facultative anaerobe that gains entry through skin wounds contaminated by soil or freshwater. It survives and multiplies within phagocytes because it resists the oxidative burst, which explains the marked susceptibility of people with chronic granulomatous disease and other neutrophil-function defects. Virulence factors including a type III secretion system and cytotoxins allow the organism to disseminate haematogenously, seeding the liver, lungs, spleen and other organs with abscesses. The combination of intracellular survival and abscess formation underlies its tendency toward fulminant, relapsing sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated fungal infection in immunocompromised hosts
Other Gram-negative bacteraemias with soft-tissue involvement
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures and culture of pus or tissue, watching for violet-pigmented colonies
Gram stain of aspirate showing Gram-negative bacilli
Cross-sectional imaging (ultrasound or CT) to detect hepatic, splenic and pulmonary abscesses
Dihydrorhodamine or nitroblue tetrazolium testing to screen for chronic granulomatous disease
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide directed therapy given variable resistance
Inflammatory markers and organ-function panels to assess systemic severity
redFlags: Rapidly progressive sepsis after soil or freshwater exposure in a tropical setting
Multiple visceral abscesses on imaging in a febrile patient
Recurrent bacterial infections suggesting an underlying phagocyte defect
Deteriorating haemodynamics despite initial antibiotic therapy
reference.prognosis: Localised skin infection may resolve with drainage and antibiotics, but disseminated disease carries substantial mortality; outcome improves with early recognition, appropriate agents chosen for the organism's resistance pattern, and prolonged therapy with abscess drainage.
pitfalls: Using empirical beta-lactams to which the organism is commonly resistant
Stopping therapy too early and precipitating relapse from residual abscesses
Failing to investigate an underlying immune defect after severe or recurrent infection
Dismissing an apparently trivial skin lesion in a systemically unwell patient
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
